# Fine-hyperplane nonconcentration forces normalized sampling recovery

This note supplies a bridge complementary to
`candidate a779c844eb8df3e4`. That theorem finds a
large actual hyperplane when coarse volume is small relative to sampled
mass. Here a VANISHING maximum hyperplane fraction forces dense
sampling after block shape normalization. The merely weaker condition
that no hyperplane carries half the mass does not suffice for density.

The resulting recovery theorem derives its retained support and its
discarded-fine-mass condition from the original fine law. It makes no
initial assumption that the positive COARSE limiting weights coincide
with the positive FINE limiting weights.

## 1. An elementary Euclidean lattice transference bound

For a full-rank lattice L in R^r, write rho(L) for covering radius,
L* for its dual, and lambda_1(L*) for the shortest nonzero dual norm.
Let kappa_r be the unit Euclidean ball volume. Then

    rho(L) lambda_1(L*) <= C_r:=r 2^(r-1)/kappa_r.        (1)

Only a dimension-dependent constant is needed; in particular
C_r<=r^(r+1)/2 follows from the cube [-1/r,1/r]^r in the unit ball.

Here is a direct proof. Choose lattice vectors v_1,...,v_r greedily,
each of smallest norm outside the span of its predecessors. Their
norms are the successive minima lambda_1<=...<=lambda_r: among any
i independent vectors of norm at most lambda_i, one is outside the
previous (i-1)-span, and the greedy first i vectors prove the reverse
inequality. Use an orthonormal basis adapted to the resulting flag.
Let D divide coordinate i by lambda_i.

For any nonzero lattice vector x, let j be its highest nonzero flag
coordinate. Then x is outside the first (j-1)-span, so |x|>=lambda_j.
All its nonzero coordinates have divisors at most lambda_j; hence
|Dx|>=|x|/lambda_j>=1. The open radius-1/2 balls around D L are
disjoint. Integrating one such ball modulo a fundamental cell gives

    kappa_r/2^r <= det(D L)=det(L)/product_i lambda_i.

Thus product_i lambda_i<=2^r det(L)/kappa_r. Define the nonzero
linear functional

    w dot x=det(v_1,...,v_(r-1),x)/det(L),

with a consistent orientation. Its value on L is integral, because
all columns are lattice vectors. Therefore w belongs to L*, and

    |w|<=product_(i<r) lambda_i/det(L)
        <=2^r/[kappa_r lambda_r].

For r=1 the numerator is the empty determinant and the same formula
holds. The sublattice generated by all v_i has a fundamental
parallelepiped within distance (1/2)sum_i |v_i| of its origin after
rounding its coefficients. Since that sublattice is contained in L,
rho(L)<=r lambda_r/2. Combining with the bound on |w| proves (1).
This argument requires no sharp Gaussian transference theorem.

## 2. A quantitative concentration-to-mesh inequality

Let a finite positive measure be supported on fine lattice fibers
over a coset a+L, with its fine base projection contained in a ball
of radius R in R^r. Let xi<1 be its maximum fraction on an affine
hyperplane of the fine base. Then

    rho(L) <= 2 C_r R xi/(1-xi).                         (2)

Indeed for any nonzero v in L*, the possible levels v dot u lie
in a translate of Z. The support meets at most 2R|v|+1 such levels.
Each corresponding affine hyperplane has mass at most xi of the
total, so 1<=xi(2R|v|+1). Taking a shortest dual vector yields
lambda_1(L*)>=(xi^(-1)-1)/(2R), and (1) proves (2).

This uses actual positive mass, not the number of geometric base
points. Atoms and closed supporting hyperplanes are allowed. Coset
translations do not change the estimate. A block map
(u,x)->(Au,Bu+Cx) sends fine hyperplanes bijectively to fine
hyperplanes and preserves their conditional mass fractions, since
its section Jacobian is the same at every fine base.

For later use one can replace 2C_r by the elementary integer constant
r^(r+1). In particular xi->0 in a uniformly bounded block frame
forces rho(L)->0.

### 2.1. A coupled-normal formulation invariant under coarse-to-fine shears

For any finite positive measure supported on at most J coarse levels
z in R^k, let eta_u be its maximum normalized mass on a fine-only
hyperplane b dot u=c, b nonzero. Let eta_coupled instead allow every
hyperplane

    a dot z + b dot u = c,       b nonzero.

Then, without any convexity or sampling assumption,

    eta_u <= eta_coupled <= min{1,J eta_u}.               (2a)

The first inequality sets a=0. For the second, fix one coupled
hyperplane. On each coarse level z its trace is a fine hyperplane
b dot u=c-a dot z. Its mass on that level is at most the mass on
the same fine hyperplane across ALL levels, hence at most eta_u
times the total mass. Summing over at most J levels proves (2a).

The coupled family is preserved bijectively by every invertible
flag-preserving affine change

    z'=U z+z_0,       u'=A u+B z+u_0,

with U and A invertible. A nonzero b remains nonzero after pullback.
Consequently eta_coupled is exactly invariant for the pushed-forward
normalized measure. This is a statement about the measures and
hyperplanes; an arbitrary B need not preserve a single common
fine-lattice coset, and can produce level-dependent coset offsets.

With J uniformly bounded, eta_u tending to zero is therefore
equivalent to eta_coupled tending to zero. The hypothesis (4) can
be replaced by this coupled-normal condition. In particular its
vanishing is invariant under coarse-to-fine affine shears, even
though the numerical value of eta_u need not be.

The factor J is exact. For r=k=1, the full-dimensional tube

    0<=z<=J-1,       |u-z|<=epsilon<1/2,       x in K,

sampled at integer z,u, has exactly J equal positive fibers, at
(z,u)=(j,j). Its fine-only maximum is 1/J, while the coupled plane
u-z=0 has all the mass. Here J>=2 and K is any positive-dimensional
convex body. This also shows why a uniform bound on J is needed
for equivalence of the two vanishing conditions.

## 3. Setting for the original fine source

Let k>=0, r>=1, s>=0 and m=r+s. Let C_l be compact convex sources
in R^k_z times R^r_u times R^s_x. Assume all nonempty coarse integer
fibers have indices in one FIXED finite set P subset Z^k. Individual
coarse fibers may initially be empty or lower dimensional. Use a
full-rank fine lattice coset a_l+L_l, of covolume v_l, and let

    mu_l=v_l sum_(z in P,u in a_l+L_l)
                          H_s restricted to (C_l)_(z,u),
    T_l=mu_l(total)>0.

For s=0 this is covolume-weighted counting. Define

    eta_l=sup_(affine hyperplanes E subset R^r)
                        mu_l({u in E})/T_l.             (3)

These are hyperplanes in the FINE u coordinates alone. They are
not arbitrary hyperplanes in all integer coordinates (z,u): a
coarse-level hyperplane could carry fixed positive mass and would
make that stronger condition inappropriate with finite P.

Assume

    eta_l ->0.                                          (4)

After taking a subsequence, all coarse FINE mass fractions converge:

    mu_(l,z)(total)/T_l -> alpha_z,
    E={z in P:alpha_z>0}.

They sum to one. The conclusions proved below are:

* E is lattice-convex, and its retained fibers are eventually full
  m-dimensional convex bodies.
* If M_(l,z) is their ordinary m-volume, then
  mu_(l,z)(total)/M_(l,z)->1 for every z in E.
* M_(l,E):=sum_(z in E)M_(l,z) satisfies M_(l,E)/T_l->1.
  The discarded fine mass divided by M_(l,E) tends to zero.
* Every retained dependence component admits the block maps in
  the compact full-shape theorem with transformed fine covering
  radii tending to zero.

Thus all hypotheses needed by
`candidate 5ef2792a4d153635`
are derived on the retained family, including the mass condition
which could not previously be inferred from zero coarse weight.

## 4. Positive fine mass gives a full shape and its sampling ratio

Fix z in E. Its own maximum fine-hyperplane fraction is at most
eta_l divided by mu_(l,z)(total)/T_l, and hence tends to zero.
In particular its positive sampled fine bases eventually do not
lie in any affine hyperplane. They have full affine rank r.

For s>=1, one positive sampled s-fiber supplies the entire vertical
R^s direction, and points over r independent base differences
supply r more directions. Its coarse convex fiber is therefore
full m-dimensional and has M_(l,z)>0. For s=0 the full-rank
sampled points directly give a full r-dimensional coarse body.

Choose a determinant-1/M_(l,z) John-type normalization of this ONE
body. Its translated image has volume one and universal positive
inner and outer radii depending only on m. As in the component
normalization note, postcompose with an orthogonal map taking the
image of {0} times R^s back to that subspace. The linear map has
block form (Au,Bu+Cx), without changing its volume or radius bounds.

The conditional fine-hyperplane fractions are invariant under this
map, so (2) makes rho(A L_l)->0. Uniform convex-set sampling in
the bounded normalized body gives its weighted fine mass tending
to its ordinary volume one. More explicitly the normalized fine
covolume is v_l |det A| and the continuous section Jacobian is
|det C|, with

    v_l |det A| |det C|=v_l/M_(l,z).

Thus that sampled mass is exactly mu_(l,z)(total)/M_(l,z).
The sampling error is bounded by
2r rho(2R+2rho)^(m-1), including s=0 and closed boundaries.
This proves the asserted ratio. Consequently

    M_(l,z)/T_l -> alpha_z>0.                           (5)

## 5. Fine-positive support closure, without an assumed coarse limit

Let j=sum_i lambda_i z_i be an integer convex combination of
retained bases, with positive fixed coefficients. For one source
z_i, convexity supplies a translated contained copy

    lambda_i (C_l)_(z_i) + t_l subset (C_l)_j.           (6)

Apply the ONE-source block normalization from Section 4. The copy
in (6), after subtracting its center, is contained in a fixed ball
and has normalized volume lambda_i^m. Its lattice coset can be
arbitrarily translated, but the same covering radius tends to zero.
The uniform sampling bound is uniform in this translation. It
therefore gives

    mu_(l,j)(total)
       >=M_(l,z_i) [lambda_i^m-o(1)].                   (7)

The target j is an actual coarse base by convexity, so it lies in
the finite universe P whenever the sources occur. Divide (7) by
T_l and use (5):

    alpha_j >= lambda_i^m alpha_(z_i)>0.

Hence j belongs to E. This proves lattice convexity of E. Once
every target is retained, ordinary Brunn--Minkowski and (5) also
give the stronger weight relation

    alpha_j^(1/m)>=sum_i lambda_i alpha_(z_i)^(1/m).

Summing (5) over E gives M_(l,E)/T_l->sum_E alpha_z=1.
By the definition of E the discarded fine mass is o(T_l), hence
also o(M_(l,E)). This establishes both the retained coarse
normalization and the required discarded-fine-mass estimate.

## 6. Component normalization and actual center recovery

In each dependence component of E select one retained anchor z.
Multiply its individual block normalization from Section 4 by
the scalar (M_(l,z)/M_(l,E))^(1/m). The determinant becomes
1/M_(l,E), and this scalar stays bounded above and below by
positive constants. Its transformed fine covering radius still
tends to zero. The positive volume ratios in (5) allow the
full-shape incidence argument to bound all other component shapes
under that SAME map. Representation-affine position correction
changes coset offsets but not the transformed lattice.

All assumptions of the transformed-component recovery theorem
therefore hold on E. If necessary first reduce its saturated
coarse affine lattice to rank k'<=k, leaving fine and continuous
coordinates unchanged. Let nu_* be a resulting compact
intrinsic full-shape lift limit along a selected subsequence I.
Then the following liminf is along that SAME subsequence:

    liminf_(l in I) D_max(original fine source_l)
                              >= D_max(nu_*).            (8)

The proof supplies actual original fine points: choose an interior
approximation to a deepest lift point, round only its residual
fine coordinates in its actual coset, and apply the affine
pullback. Uniform halfspace discrepancy and the o(T_l) discarded
mass prove (8). No integer lattice is asserted across the entire
auxiliary lift, and no OC theorem is applied to its weighted fine
cosets.

If lower-integer-rank OC is known in the continuous dimensions
needed by the full-shape lift, (8) gives the corresponding
2^(-k') Gamma_(B(k',m)) lower bound, where
B(k',m)=(m+1)2^(k')-k'-1. Every subsequence realizing a full-sequence
liminf admits the fine-weight and shape subsequences above, so a
universal such bound holds for the full original liminf.
For k'=0 the only coarse theorem needed is ordinary Grunbaum;
the limit bound is then Gamma_m. The usual strict comparison with
the original 2^(-k-r) Gamma_s target remains as in the recovery
note. These OC implications remain explicitly conditional for
positive retained coarse rank.

## 7. Why excluding a half-mass hyperplane does not itself force density

Let r=1, choose h_l>0, and take the actual body

    Q_l=[0,2h_l] times K,

where K is any positive s-dimensional convex body. Sample on
h_l Z. It has exactly three equal positive sampled fibers, so its
maximum fine-hyperplane fraction is exactly 1/3<1/2. Also
Q_l is exactly the convex hull of its sampled set. Yet after
u'=u/h_l-1, its base interval is [-1,1] and its fine lattice
spacing is one, with covering radius 1/2.

More generally, ANY block shape normalization having a uniform
inner ball of radius b>0 must have fine projection width at least
2b. Since the original width is 2h_l, its scalar fine block A
satisfies |A|h_l>=b. The transformed covering radius is therefore
at least b/2. Density cannot be repaired by another uniformly
round block frame. In the simple frame above, the inequality (2)
is exact in rank one: R=1, xi=1/3 and rho=1/2.

Thus the nonconcentration hypothesis (4) cannot be weakened merely
to eta_l<1/2 in this recovery argument. The intermediate regime
of persistent positive but sub-half hyperplane mass needs an
additional allocation or discrete argument. This counterexample
rejects that density inference; it makes no adverse depth claim.

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_fine_hyperplane_nonconcentration.py` checks the elementary
arithmetic calibrations and the exact three-slice obstruction.
For ordinary background only, the flag product bound above is the
Euclidean case of Minkowski's second theorem; a short general proof
appears in [Henk, Successive Minima and Lattice Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204158). All lattice estimates used
here were derived explicitly in Sections 1--2.

# Fine-hyperplane nonconcentration forces normalized sampling recovery

**Quantitative hyperplane concentration to lattice mesh bound**

For a full-rank lattice L in R^r, rho(L) lambda_1(L*) <= C_r=r 2^(r-1)/kappa_r. If a finite positive measure on a coset of L has base projection in a radius-R ball and maximum affine-hyperplane mass fraction xi<1, then rho(L)<=2 C_r R xi/(1-xi).

Scope limits: Mesh recovery requires xi tending to zero in uniformly bounded normalized frames. A mere sub-half concentration bound does not imply dense sampling.
